summary:
Central Sulawesi stands under the national framework of Indonesia. The sources record no separate LGBTI legislation or enforcement specific to this province, so a visitor is assessed against the national position with no documented sub-national deviation.

Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, go further and criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, and two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025. Neither regime applies in Central Sulawesi, but travel onward carries a materially different legal exposure.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Physical risk is rising across the country. Vigilante mobs attacked trans women in a nationwide wave of 14 to 16 July 2026; in Bogor more than 15 trans women were doused, stripped and beaten, with footage circulated online. Reporting of August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Documents offer no option outside the binary. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X marker, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval.
tangentialFactors:
The Constitutional Court rejected a conservative petition on 14 December 2017 by five votes to four, declining to add criminalisation of homosexuality and extramarital sex to the Penal Code. The code signed in December 2022 nonetheless reaches the same conduct through the extra-marital sex provision, which took effect on 2 January 2026.

A researcher cited in reporting of August 2026 documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016. That shift is consistent with the mob violence recorded in July 2026 and with the framing of the October 2025 presidential decree, which places LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy alongside separatism and terrorism.

Compared with Aceh, where two men were caned in February 2025 under provincial religious law, Central Sulawesi carries no documented religious-penalty regime. The difference arises from provincial law rather than from any relaxation at national level, and a visitor moving between provinces should expect enforcement to change at the provincial border.
localsOnly:
Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Constitution does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. Transgender Indonesians who do not hide their identity often struggle to keep legitimate employment and can be pushed into sex work.

A global survey cited in the sources reports that discrimination and harassment against trans Indonesians are not uncommon, while direct violence is recorded as rare. Reporting from July 2026 indicates that this balance has shifted, with organised physical attacks on trans women captured on footage and shared online.

Changing legal gender markers is a court-supervised process available only after sex reassignment surgery, which sets the terms on which residents can present consistently in public and at work.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports a Central Sulawesi-specific LGBTI finding. Whether the province has adopted regional bylaws on morality, dress or same-sex conduct, and how its police handle such matters, remains unresolved on the available record.

Enforcement frequency under the 2022 penal code inside Central Sulawesi is not sourced. The reporting available characterises prosecutions nationally as selective rather than systematic but supplies no provincial breakdown, and the Puncak raid of 22 June 2025 is the only enforcement operation described in detail, in another province.

The status of the bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour, whether it was enacted after the 2025 discussions or remains pending, is not resolved in these sources. The availability of healthcare, shelter or legal-assistance services for trans visitors in Central Sulawesi is likewise not documented here.
